# Tax-plan experiment {#sec-br}

@ballard2017structure ask how Americans evaluate federal income-tax schedules by having respondents
choose between two tax plans in each of eight tasks. Each plan sets the marginal rate in six income
brackets and states, in five categories, how much revenue it raises compared with current policy.
This chapter reproduces the paper's results from the saved fit.

```{r}
#| label: br-setup
#| cache: false
library(sconjoint)
fits <- getOption("sconjoint.fits", "fits")
br <- sc_load(file.path(fits, "br_q4.rds"))
if (is.null(br)) stop("This chapter needs the saved fit br_q4.rds; see the installation chapter.")
```

```{r}
#| label: br-knitr
#| include: false
#| cache: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(dev.args = list(pointsize = 11))
```

As in @sec-gs, the chapter loads `_figs-helpers.R`, which sets `cores` for `sc_estimate()` and
defines `pick()`.

```{r}
#| label: br-helpers
#| cache: false
#| file: _figs-helpers.R
```

## Data and fit

Calling `sc_example_data("br")` builds the paper's inputs from the bundled `br2017` data. It keeps
the 1,991 respondents who answered the income question, giving 15,928 tasks with Plan A as the first
profile. Each plan is represented by 16 coded features: each of the six rates enters utility through a
linear and a quadratic term, and the revenue category enters through four contrasts.

The network takes sixteen columns coding age, sex, education, race, income, and party ID. These
covariates were collected after the experiment; using them assumes that assignment affects neither
how they are reported nor inclusion in the valid-income sample.

```{r}
#| label: br-data
x <- sc_example_data("br")
x
table(x$groups$party, useNA = "ifany")
```

The party groups consist of Democrats (`party == "Dem"`, 885), Republicans (`party == "Rep"`, 643),
and independents (`pid7 == 4`, 389). The `party == "Ind"` category also includes the 74 respondents
who answered "not sure"; because those respondents belong to no party group, the book selects
independents by `pid7`.

The fit selected four taste factors, as summarized in the table below; reproducing it takes several
hours:

```{r}
#| label: br-fit
#| eval: false
fit_q <- lapply(1:5, function(q) sc_fit(x, q = q))
sc_select_rank(fit_q)
br <- sc_states(fit_q[[4]])                           # q = 4; M = 250 designs, 8 responses each
sc_save(br, file.path(fits, "br_q4.rds"))
```

| Taste factors | Held-out log score | Gain over $q - 1$ | Paired $z$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | -4.865 | | |
| 2 | -4.796 | 0.0696 | 5.52 |
| 3 | -4.762 | 0.0337 | 3.76 |
| 4 (selected) | -4.742 | 0.0203 | 3.59 |
| 5 | -4.746 | -0.0047 | -0.75 |

## Recorded plans

Because the displayed revenue category was generated from the six rates with noise, raising a rate
also changes the revenue a plan is likely to show. The BR helpers therefore need the plans
respondents saw, which the function below extracts from `br2017` in the order of the fitted data.

```{r}
#| label: br-profiles
br_profiles <- function(ids) {
  b <- br2017[br2017$valid_income, ]
  b <- b[order(match(b$respondent, ids), b$task), ]
  plan <- function(k) {
    z <- b[b$profile == k, ]
    data.frame(tax_rate_1_pct = z$rate_L10, tax_rate_2_pct = z$rate_10_35,
               tax_rate_3_pct = z$rate_35_85, tax_rate_4_pct = z$rate_85_175,
               tax_rate_5_pct = z$rate_175_375, tax_rate_6_pct = z$rate_375P,
               taxrev = 3 - z$revenue_score)
  }
  list(A = plan(1), B = plan(2))
}
prof <- br_profiles(br$data$data$ids)
sapply(prof, nrow)
```

## Rate changes

To evaluate a rate increase in a single bracket, `sc_br_revenue_contrast()` moves that bracket's
rate from the bottom to the top of its menu --- for example, from 5% to 55% for incomes above
\$375,000. It averages the other five rates over the contexts respondents saw and lets the displayed
revenue follow the revenue rule. The result is a vector of 16 coefficients, and setting
`per_point = TRUE` divides it by the change in the rate so that the mean measures utility per
percentage point.

```{r}
#| label: br-contrast
top <- sc_br_revenue_contrast(6, profiles = prof, per_point = TRUE)
round(top, 4)
```

In this vector, the rate part sits in `tax6_linear` --- the quadratic term cancels because the
menu's endpoints are symmetric --- while the revenue part captures the average change in the revenue
codes caused by the rate increase. Applying the same contrast to each bracket estimates the mean
utility change per percentage point across all six brackets:

```{r}
#| label: br-means
brackets <- c("under $10k", "$10-35k", "$35-85k", "$85-175k", "$175-375k", "over $375k")
contrast <- lapply(1:6, function(j) sc_br_revenue_contrast(j, profiles = prof, per_point = TRUE))
means <- sc_estimate(br, lapply(1:6, function(j) sc_mean(brackets[j], contrast[[j]])))
print(means, digits = 4)
```

On average, higher rates lower utility in the bottom three brackets and raise it in the top two: per
rate point, the penalty below \$10,000 is -0.0577, whereas the gain above \$375,000 is 0.0221.
`sc_ratio()` compares the two and attaches a delta-method interval:

```{r}
#| label: br-ratio
ratio <- sc_ratio("bottom penalty / top gain", sc_mean("bottom", contrast[[1]]),
                  sc_mean("top", contrast[[6]]))
sc_estimate(br, ratio)
```

In relative terms, the bottom-bracket penalty is 2.61 times the top-bracket gain.

## Preference shares

A preference share measures the fraction of respondents whose utility change, averaged over
contexts, is positive. Because each share requires a bounded update, the targets below run in
parallel.

```{r}
#| label: br-shares
top_55_35 <- sc_br_revenue_contrast(6, high = 55, low = 35, profiles = prof)
shares <- sc_estimate(br, c(
  lapply(1:6, function(j) sc_share(brackets[j], contrast[[j]])),
  list(sc_share("top rate 35% to 55%", top_55_35),
       sc_mean("top rate 35% to 55%: mean", top_55_35))), cores = cores)
print(shares, digits = 4)
```

Across the full menu range, an estimated 69.1% favor raising the top rate from 5% to 55%, and 54.7%
favor the higher rate in the \$85,000--\$175,000 bracket. Even in the \$10,000--\$35,000 bracket,
where the mean utility change is negative, 29.2% favor the higher rate.

Raising the top rate from 35% to 55%, however, splits respondents evenly, with a share of 49.7% and
a mean of -0.013 whose interval includes zero. Because utility is quadratic in each rate, the
direction of a taste can depend on where a change starts.

## By party

Subgroup estimates are defined by passing a function of the respondent groups that returns the
subgroup weights:

```{r}
#| label: br-party
party_w <- list(Democrats = function(g) g$party == "Dem", independents = function(g) g$pid7 == 4,
                Republicans = function(g) g$party == "Rep")
party_targets <- list()
for (j in c(1, 6)) for (p in names(party_w))
  party_targets[[length(party_targets) + 1]] <-
    sc_share(paste(brackets[j], p, sep = ", "), contrast[[j]], w = party_w[[p]])
party_shares <- sc_estimate(br, party_targets, cores = cores)
party_shares
```

On raising the top rate, 83.5% of Democrats favor the increase compared with 52.8% of Republicans,
whose interval includes 50%. On raising the bottom rate, by contrast, all three groups sit far below
50%.

```{r}
#| label: fig-br-party-shares
#| fig-cap: "Preference shares by party"
#| fig-width: 7.2
#| fig-height: 3.4
by_party <- function(p) {             # one party's rows, named by bracket
  z <- pick(party_shares, paste(brackets[c(1, 6)], p, sep = ", ")); z$name <- brackets[c(1, 6)]; z
}
sc_plot_estimates(Democrat = by_party("Democrats"), Independent = by_party("independents"),
                  Republican = by_party("Republicans"), scale = 100, xlim = c(0, 100),
                  labels = c("Below $10k", "Above $375k"),
                  xlab = "Share favoring the higher rate (%)")
```

The plotted bars show 95% log-odds intervals, and the party groups include leaners.

The one-step correction widens the party gap on the top rate: before correction (`plug_in`), the
shares are 76.8% for Democrats and 63.8% for Republicans, a smaller gap than in the corrected shares
above.

The difference between the two party means can also be estimated with its own interval:

```{r}
#| label: br-gap
gap <- sc_difference("top rate: Democrats minus Republicans",
                     sc_mean("Democrats", contrast[[6]], w = party_w$Democrats),
                     sc_mean("Republicans", contrast[[6]], w = party_w$Republicans))
print(sc_estimate(br, gap), digits = 4)
```

## Fitted distributions

To examine the full distribution of tastes across respondents, `sc_fitted_law()` computes the fitted
law of the utility change per rate point for each bracket.

```{r}
#| label: br-laws
laws <- lapply(contrast, function(cc) sc_fitted_law(br, cc))
bn <- c("Below $10k", "$10-35k", "$35-85k", "$85-175k", "$175-375k", "Above $375k")
```

The top bracket's law is narrower than the bottom bracket's, with about 30% of its mass
below zero. As in @sec-gs, the curves come before the one-step correction, so the vertical line at
each corrected mean need not sit at a curve's center.

```{r}
#| label: fig-br-distributions
#| fig-cap: "Fitted preferences over tax-rate changes"
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5.8
sc_plot_laws(laws, labels = bn, means = pick(means, brackets), height = 1.3, bins = 300,
             outline = "line", xlab = "Utility per percentage point of tax rate")
```

To isolate tastes for the displayed revenue alone, each contrast holds the tax rates fixed and
compares a revenue category with "about the same" revenue. The revenue category (`taxrev`: 1 = much
more revenue, 3 = about the same, 5 = much less) enters through four Helmert columns, each scaled to
mean square one. In the code below, row `k` of `H` codes category `k`; subtracting row 3 from row
`k`, with zero rate coefficients, gives its contrast relative to "about the same".

```{r}
#| label: br-revenue-laws
H <- contr.helmert(5); H <- sweep(H, 2, sqrt(colSums(H^2) / 5), "/")
revenue_contrast <- function(k) setNames(c(rep(0, 12), H[k, ] - H[3, ]), br$data$data$feature_names)
revenue_laws <- lapply(c(5, 4, 2, 1), function(k) sc_fitted_law(br, revenue_contrast(k)))
```

Unlike the rate figure above, the figure below plots the fitted distributions without corrected
means.

```{r}
#| label: fig-br-revenue-distributions
#| fig-cap: "Fitted preferences over displayed revenue"
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.4
sc_plot_laws(revenue_laws, labels = c("Much less revenue", "Less revenue", "More revenue",
                                      "Much more revenue"),
             height = 1.3, bins = 300, outline = "line",
             xlab = "Utility relative to about the same revenue")
```

## Complete tax plans

Rather than changing one bracket at a time, `sc_br_plan_contest()` compares two complete plans,
setting position effects to zero and keeping task shocks. Because each plan's revenue category is
drawn from the revenue rule, the contest averages over the categories both plans could show. The
paper uses four plans:

| Plan | Under \$10k | \$10--35k | \$35--85k | \$85--175k | \$175--375k | Over \$375k |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Progressive | 0 | 5 | 15 | 25 | 35 | 45 |
| Flat | 15 | 15 | 15 | 15 | 15 | 15 |
| Status-quo analogue | 5 | 15 | 25 | 25 | 35 | 35 |
| Regressive | 25 | 25 | 15 | 15 | 5 | 5 |

The paper reports all six pairs, both for all respondents and for each party group. Because support
for the second plan is one minus that of the first, the chunk below estimates each pair once and
adds the reversed rows.

```{r}
#| label: br-contests
rates <- rbind(progressive = c(0, 5, 15, 25, 35, 45), flat = rep(15, 6),
               status_quo = c(5, 15, 25, 25, 35, 35), regressive = c(25, 25, 15, 15, 5, 5))
groups <- c(list(all = NULL), party_w)
pairs <- t(combn(4, 2))
plan_targets <- list(); meta <- list()
for (i in seq_len(nrow(pairs))) for (p in names(groups)) {
  a <- rownames(rates)[pairs[i, 1]]; b <- rownames(rates)[pairs[i, 2]]
  plan_targets[[length(plan_targets) + 1]] <-
    sc_br_plan_contest(paste(a, "vs", b, p, sep = ", "), rates[a, ], rates[b, ], w = groups[[p]])
  meta[[length(meta) + 1]] <- data.frame(plan = a, opponent = b, group = p)
}
plans <- sc_estimate(br, plan_targets)
support <- cbind(do.call(rbind, meta), plans[c("estimate", "lower", "upper")])
support <- rbind(support, transform(support, plan = opponent, opponent = plan, estimate = 1 - estimate,
                                    lower = 1 - upper, upper = 1 - lower))
progressive <- support[support$plan == "progressive", ]
wide <- round(100 * tapply(progressive$estimate, progressive[c("opponent", "group")], sum), 1)
wide[rownames(rates)[2:4], names(groups)]
```

The progressive plan has an estimated expected support of 69.5% against the flat plan, 59.6% against
the status-quo analogue, and 81.0% against the regressive plan. Against the flat plan, it draws
79.3% among Democrats and 58.3% among Republicans. Among the other pairings, the status-quo analogue
draws 65.1% against the flat plan, and the flat plan draws 82.6% against the regressive plan.

In the figure below, Panel A shows the four schedules, while Panels B to E show each plan's support
against the other three, with whiskers marking 95% log-odds intervals and a dashed line at 50%.

```{r}
#| label: fig-br-contests
#| fig-cap: "Expected support for complete tax plans"
#| fig-width: 8.2
#| fig-height: 8.8
par(las = 1, tcl = -.2, mgp = c(1.7, .45, 0), xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i", ps = 12)
layout(matrix(c(1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 6), 4, byrow = TRUE), heights = c(2.1, 3.05, 3.05, .6))
par(mar = c(3, 4, 2.3, 1))
plot(NA, xlim = c(1, 6), ylim = c(0, 60), xlab = "Income bracket (lowest to highest)",
     ylab = "Tax rate (%)", axes = FALSE)
abline(h = seq(0, 60, 15), col = "#E8E8E8"); axis(1, at = 1:6); axis(2, at = seq(0, 60, 15))
title("A. Tax schedules", line = .8, cex.main = 1)
plan_cols <- c(blue, "#777777", green, red)
for (j in 1:4) lines(1:6, rates[j, ], col = plan_cols[j], lty = j, lwd = 1.5)
legend("topleft", c("Progressive", "Flat 15%", "Status quo", "Regressive"),
       col = plan_cols, lty = 1:4, lwd = 1.5, bty = "n", cex = .85, horiz = TRUE)
plan_labels <- c("Progressive", "Flat", "Status quo", "Regressive")
bar_cols <- c("#333333", cols)
for (j in 1:4) {
  opponents <- setdiff(1:4, j)
  par(mar = c(3.1, 6.2, 2.25, 1.1))
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 100), ylim = c(.5, 3.5), axes = FALSE, xlab = "Expected support (%)", ylab = "")
  abline(v = seq(0, 100, 25), col = "#E8E8E8", lwd = .6)
  axis(1, at = seq(0, 100, 25), cex.axis = .9)
  axis(2, at = 3:1, labels = paste("vs.", plan_labels[opponents]), tick = FALSE, cex.axis = .9)
  title(paste0(LETTERS[j + 1L], ". ", plan_labels[j], " plan"), line = .65, cex.main = 1)
  for (k in 1:4) {
    z <- support[support$plan == rownames(rates)[j] & support$group == names(groups)[k], ]
    z <- z[match(rownames(rates)[opponents], z$opponent), ]
    y <- 3:1 + c(.27, .09, -.09, -.27)[k]
    rect(0, y - .07, 100 * z$estimate, y + .07, col = bar_cols[k], border = NA)
    for (h in 1:2) {                 # whiskers: a white halo, then a dark line
      ink <- c("white", "#111111")[h]; width <- c(2.2, .8)[h]
      segments(100 * z$lower, y, 100 * z$upper, y, col = ink, lwd = width)
      segments(100 * z$lower, y - .035, 100 * z$lower, y + .035, col = ink, lwd = width)
      segments(100 * z$upper, y - .035, 100 * z$upper, y + .035, col = ink, lwd = width)
    }
  }
  abline(v = 50, lty = 2, col = "#666666", lwd = .8)
}
par(mar = rep(0, 4)); plot.new()
legend("center", c("All respondents", "Democrat", "Independent", "Republican"),
       fill = bar_cols, border = NA, bty = "n", horiz = TRUE, cex = .9)
```

## Effects on choices

To measure how single-bracket rate changes affect choices, `sc_br_endpoint_ame()` gives the AME of
moving one bracket's rate from the bottom to the top of its menu, redrawing the focal plan's revenue
category from the revenue rule while leaving the opponent as recorded. Because the calculation
covers both sides of all 15,928 recorded tasks --- about 90,000 contest rows --- each bracket takes
about 20 minutes.

```{r}
#| label: br-ames
ames <- sc_estimate(br, lapply(1:6, function(j) sc_br_endpoint_ame(brackets[j], j, profiles = prof)),
                      cores = min(6L, parallel::detectCores()))
ames
```

Raising the bottom rate from 0% to 25% lowers a plan's expected support by 18.8 percentage points,
whereas raising the top rate from 5% to 55% raises it by 14.1.

The main figure brings all four summaries together for each bracket: mean utility per rate point
(A), fitted law (B), share favoring the higher rate (C), and AME of the endpoint switch (D).

```{r}
#| label: fig-br-preferences
#| fig-cap: "Preferences over tax-rate changes"
#| fig-width: 9.2
#| fig-height: 4.1
ame_ticks <- pretty(range(0, 100 * ames$lower, 100 * ames$upper), n = 3)
sc_plot_preferences(means, laws, shares, ames, labels = bn, order = brackets, hide_wide = FALSE,
                    xlim = list(A = c(-.08, .05), B = c(-.3, .2), D = range(ame_ticks)),
                    # ticks off the panels' edges, so neighbouring labels do not touch
                    ticks = list(A = c(-.06, 0, .04), B = c(-.2, -.1, 0, .1), D = head(ame_ticks[-1], -1)),
                    titles = list(A = "A. Mean utility\nper rate point"),
                    widths = c(1.85, 1.6, 1.7, 1.6, 1.8))
```

All intervals are 95%: Wald intervals for means and AMEs, and log-odds intervals for shares.

The same bracket-level estimates can also be displayed as a table:

```{r}
#| label: br-table
#| results: asis
sc_table("Mean per point" = means, "Share favoring" = shares, "Choice effect" = ames,
         order = brackets, labels = bn, digits = 3, format = "markdown", n = TRUE)
```

## Decisiveness

A bracket's decisiveness is how often exchanging two plans' rates in that bracket would reverse the
choice, keeping the other rates, the displayed revenue, and the task shock as recorded. To compute
it, `sc_decisiveness()` takes each bracket's two coded columns together with a menu containing one
row per rate.

In the code below, each menu row takes the rate part of `sc_br_revenue_contrast()`
(`follow_revenue = FALSE`) for a move from the bracket's lowest rate to that rate. Anchoring every
row at the lowest rate does not affect the result, because adding the same vector to every row
leaves every pairwise swap unchanged.

```{r}
#| label: br-decisiveness
menu <- function(j, menu_rates) {
  cols <- paste0("tax", j, c("_linear", "_quadratic"))
  t(sapply(menu_rates, function(r)
    sc_br_revenue_contrast(j, r, menu_rates[1], profiles = prof, follow_revenue = FALSE)[cols]))
}
dec <- sc_estimate(br, sc_decisiveness(
  list(top = c("tax6_linear", "tax6_quadratic"), bottom = c("tax1_linear", "tax1_quadratic")),
  menus = list(top = menu(6, c(5, 15, 25, 35, 45, 55)), bottom = menu(1, c(0, 5, 15, 25))),
  pairs = list(top = rbind(c(6L, 1L), c(6L, 4L)), bottom = rbind(c(4L, 1L))),
  names = c("top rate: 55 vs 5", "top rate: 55 vs 35", "bottom rate: 25 vs 0")))
dec
```

Exchanging top rates of 55% and 5% between two plans would reverse an estimated 45.4% of choices,
whereas exchanging 55% and 35% would reverse only 15.7%. For the bottom bracket, exchanging rates of
25% and 0% would reverse 50.5%. This calculation took about eight minutes.

## All paper targets

The paper's main results file for this experiment has 43 rows, which `br_targets()` assembles in a
single list. The list includes a mean and a share for each bracket contrast, the bracket 1 and 6
contrasts by party, the 35% to 55% top-rate change (both with revenue following the rule and with
revenue fixed), the 5% to 25% bottom-rate change, the twelve plan contests, the ratio, and the party
difference.

```{r}
#| label: br-full
br_targets <- function(st, prof) {
  g <- st$data$groups; n <- st$data$data$n
  groups <- list(Dem = as.numeric(g$party == "Dem"), Ind = as.numeric(g$pid7 == 4),
                 Rep = as.numeric(g$party == "Rep"))
  party <- c(list(all = rep(1, n)), groups)
  tl <- list(); add <- function(t) tl[[length(tl) + 1L]] <<- t
  add_mean_share <- function(name, c, w = NULL) {
    add(sc_mean(paste0(name, ".mean"), c, w)); add(sc_share(paste0(name, ".share"), c, w))
  }
  for (j in 1:6) {
    cc <- sc_br_revenue_contrast(j, profiles = prof, per_point = TRUE)
    add_mean_share(paste0("bracket", j), cc)
    if (j %in% c(1L, 6L)) for (gg in names(groups)) add_mean_share(paste0("bracket", j, ".", gg), cc, groups[[gg]])
  }
  add_mean_share("top55v35", sc_br_revenue_contrast(6, 55, 35, prof))
  add(sc_mean("top55v35.fixed", sc_br_revenue_contrast(6, 55, 35, prof, follow_revenue = FALSE)))
  add_mean_share("bottom25v5", sc_br_revenue_contrast(1, 25, 5, prof))
  rates <- rbind(progressive = c(0, 5, 15, 25, 35, 45), flat = rep(15, 6),
                 sq = c(5, 15, 25, 25, 35, 35), reg = c(25, 25, 15, 15, 5, 5))
  for (alt in 2:4) for (gg in names(party))
    add(sc_br_plan_contest(paste0("contest.", rownames(rates)[alt], ".", gg), rates[1L, ], rates[alt, ],
                           w = party[[gg]]))
  c1 <- sc_br_revenue_contrast(1, profiles = prof, per_point = TRUE)
  c6 <- sc_br_revenue_contrast(6, profiles = prof, per_point = TRUE)
  add(sc_ratio("ratio.bottom.top", sc_mean("bracket1.mean", c1), sc_mean("bracket6.mean", c6)))
  add(sc_difference("top.DemMinusRep", sc_mean("bracket6.Dem.mean", c6, groups$Dem),
                    sc_mean("bracket6.Rep.mean", c6, groups$Rep)))
  tl
}
```

Evaluating the full list with `sc_estimate(br, br_targets(br, prof))` takes about eight minutes,
with most of that time spent on the bounded updates for the 16 shares.
